<issue>Issue Title: [FEATURE] Support MCP Tasks (SEP-1686) with MCPClient
Description:
### Problem Statement
MCP just released a new specification with the ability to have long running tasks, and to poll for results with a taskId. Without this feature, it is quite complex to handle long running tasks.
See https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/issues/1686 and https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/pull/1732
### Proposed Solution
Implement Task handling in the `MCPClient`.
At the moment the MCP python SDK is not fully ready, see https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/pull/1645
### Use Case
When agent needs MCP tools that take too long to answer synchronously (long data processing for example), the agent would trigger the task and then poll the server to know when a task is finished.
### Alternatives Solutions
Manually handle a set of tools (start / poll / get_result)
### Additional Context
_No response_

1. What does this part of the code do?

This part of the code defines the MCPClient class inside the src/strands/tools/mcp/mcp_client.py file. The MCPClient class appears to be a client interface to interact with MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools. It provides several methods such as start, stop, list_tools_sync, call_tool_sync, and utility functions for handling tool execution, background tasks, and content mapping. It also manages consumers and session activity.

2. What is the relationship between this part of the code and the bug?

The issue is about supporting MCP long-running tasks as specified by SEP-1686 in MCPClient. Given that MCPClient already has several synchronous tool call methods and utility functions, it is the right class to extend with support for starting tasks asynchronously, polling for task status using a taskId, and retrieving the results when tasks complete. This class is the main client through which tools are invoked, so enhancing it to support long-running task management is crucial for the feature.

3. Given the issue description, what would be the intended behavior of this part of the code?

The intended behavior is to add methods or extend existing ones in MCPClient to:

- Trigger long-running MCP tasks asynchronously.
- Poll the server for task status using the taskId returned by the initial trigger.
- Retrieve the results of completed tasks.
- Possibly manage task lifecycle, error handling, and timeout handling related to MCP tasks.

This will enable users of MCPClient to work with long-running MCP tools without complicating manual task start/poll/get_result flows. The feature will improve usability and align MCPClient with the MCP SEP-1686 long-running task standard.

1. What does this part of the code do?

The `call_tool_sync` method synchronously calls a tool on the MCP server by internally invoking an asynchronous call_tool method on the MCP session. It waits for the tool execution to complete and then converts the result into an MCPToolResult format. It also handles tool execution errors gracefully. This is the existing synchronous method used to invoke MCP tools.

2. What is the relationship between this part of the code and the bug?

Since the issue involves adding support for long-running MCP tasks with a taskId, this method is directly relevant because it is the existing entry point for tool invocation. However, currently, it only supports synchronous blocking calls that wait for task completion. The new feature will require additions or modifications to this method (or supplementary methods) to support asynchronous task triggering, status polling, and result fetching.

3. Given the issue description, what would be the intended behavior of this part of the code?

The intended behavior here would be either:

- To extend `call_tool_sync` to detect when a tool invocation results in a long-running task (e.g., returns a taskId) and then handle polling internally until task completion, or

- To implement additional MCPClient methods dedicated to starting tasks and polling for their completion asynchronously, leaving this method unchanged for simple synchronous calls.

Regardless of approach, existing synchronous calls for short-running tools should continue working unchanged.
